Charter Communications (CHTR) stock trades at 0.28 times its sales, against 3.2 times for the S&P 500. On earnings, the gap is narrower: 11.2 times, against the index's 21.9. Charter also carries $110 billion of debt. Shareholders paying even that low price need to know what they are buying, and the company's priorities have changed. In its fiscal Q1 2025 call, management talked up Charter's mobile business. On its November 6, 2026 call, management still called Charter the fastest-growing mobile provider in its footprint. But it now puts internet growth ahead of mobile. So what does Charter's management emphasize now, and why does it matter to you?

Charter Now Puts Winning Internet Customers First

On the fiscal Q3 2026 call, management said its top priority is to return to growth in its core business by winning more internet customers. Mobile now plays a supporting part: executives described the mobile and video products as offerings that support internet customer growth.

That is a change from the fiscal Q1 2025 call, when management said Charter would continue to be the fastest-growing mobile provider in the US. During that presentation, management credited a strong contribution from mobile growth for lifting its EBITDA growth, a profit measure before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, to 4.8%. Mobile has not left the conversation. Legacy Charter, the business the company ran before its Cox deal closed on August 19, 2026, grew its mobile lines by nearly 15% over the last twelve months. Mobile's role has changed from the growth story to a product that helps sell internet.

How Big Is Internet Next To Mobile For Charter?

Internet is the far bigger business. It brought in $23.8 billion in fiscal 2025, accounting for 43.4% of Charter's revenue that year. Mobile service brought in $3.76 billion, or 6.9% of revenue.

While mobile is the faster grower, its expansion is slowing. Mobile service revenue grew 22.0% in fiscal 2025, down from 37.4% a year earlier. Internet revenue grew just 1.7% that year.

The internet business is also losing customers faster. Legacy Charter lost 156,000 internet customers in the third quarter of 2026, more than the 109,000 it lost a year earlier. Management has therefore turned its attention to the business with the largest share of revenue, which is also where customer losses have grown.

Is Charter's New Focus Good News For You?

For now, the shift looks more concerning than reassuring. Pointing the company at its largest business makes sense on size alone, but that business is where customers are leaving faster, and management said it was not satisfied with the third quarter's result in internet customers.

A follow-up to How Much Could You Lose In AT&T Stock? (Oct 29).

On November 2 the AT&T dividend landed in brokerage accounts: 27.75 cents a share, or $277.50 for every 1,000 shares. For a retiree, that deposit is the whole reason to own the stock. Eight days later October's inflation report came in hot, prices up 0.4% against 0.3% expected, and futures raised the odds of a bigger, half-point Fed hike in December. The better question, which we'll come back to: what's your plan for that income, whatever the Fed does?

AT&T closed Thursday at $22.18, 24% below its 52-week high and down 9.4% over the past year, dividends included. At $1.11 a year in dividends, that's a yield of about 5.0%. When we asked two weeks ago how much you could lose, the answer was its worst fall since 2007: in the 2008-09 crisis, AT&T fell 45%.

That 45% is the income decision a hot CPI forces. For a seven-figure investor, a $200,000 AT&T stake pays $10,000 a year but could lose $90,000 in a 2008 repeat. Hold or trim? A Trefis partner firm can weigh it in a free 30-minute call.

Why Does A Hot CPI Hit AT&T?

Yield and debt. The 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.10% on Thursday, above AT&T's dividend yield, and a bond doesn't come with a price war. Net debt was $149.8 billion after the EchoStar spectrum deal, and AT&T doesn't expect leverage back at its 2.5x target until 2029. Each refinancing costs more as rates rise.

The business is fine: third-quarter revenue rose 5.3%, and AT&T kept its 2026 free-cash-flow outlook at $18 billion or more. Over the 12 months to September, free cash flow covered the dividend about 2.2 times. The pressure is wireless competition, with SpaceX planning to turn on a phone service in early 2028:

Key Takeaways

Elon Musk said SpaceX could "just acquire that legacy telco" if it can make better use of a carrier's spectrum, which puts AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile in the frame.

EchoStar sold SpaceX its AWS-4 and H-block licenses for about $17 billion, with up to $8.5 billion of the price paid in SpaceX stock valued at $212 a share.

That stock gives EchoStar shareholders a share of SpaceX's upside, from mobile and from the AI compute business that now brings in more than half of SpaceX's revenue.

The risk sits with Boost Mobile, which AT&T and T-Mobile would reportedly push off their spectrum if Musk moves to take it over.

SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ) has spent the past year buying spectrum for a phone service. Now Elon Musk is floating a faster way to get more. (Buy the phone company.)

Musk's comments were featured on this week's episode of the Moonshots podcast with Peter Diamandis:

"I think SpaceX will be able to get very far with the spectrum that it's acquired. But, you know, at a certain point, if we're able to make much better use of the spectrum than, say, a legacy telco is, we could just acquire that legacy telco and use the spectrum, you know, 10 times more effectively."

The obvious targets are the big carriers: AT&T (T:NYSE), Verizon (VZ:NYSE) and T-Mobile (TMUS:NASDAQ). But I'd look first at EchoStar (ECHO:NASDAQ), which sold SpaceX much of the spectrum Musk is talking about and took a big part of the price in SpaceX stock.

EchoStar already has a piece of Musk's plan

In September 2025, EchoStar agreed to sell its AWS-4 and H-block licenses to SpaceX for about $17 billion. Up to $8.5 billion of that is paid in SpaceX stock, valued at $212 a share in the agreement. The FCC approved the sale in May.

SpaceX is still adding spectrum. On Nov. 10, the FCC accepted its filing to buy 800 MHz licenses from Grain Management, a deal the Wall Street Journal reported could cost $8 billion.

So every step SpaceX takes toward a full phone business builds on the licenses EchoStar sold it, from more spectrum to buying a carrier outright. AT&T and Verizon face a new rival, while EchoStar is being paid in that rival's stock.

Mobile is only part of what EchoStar is getting

Space Exploration Technologies Corp. SPCX and AST SpaceMobile, Inc. ASTS are two key players in satellite-based communications aiming to develop extensive low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks to deliver seamless broadband and direct-to-device mobile connectivity. Operating a fleet of nearly 11,200 satellites in LEO, SpaceX's Starlink offers satellite Internet directly to consumers and business enterprises. The network served about 13.6 million Starlink subscribers across more than 150 countries and other markets. SpaceX reported a median residential download speed of 225 Mbps during peak hours.

AST SpaceMobile is building the world's first and only global cellular broadband network in space, accessible directly by standard smartphones (4G-LTE/5G devices) for commercial and government use, leveraging its extensive Intellectual Property and patent portfolio. The SpaceMobile Service is provided by a constellation of high-powered, large phased-array satellites in LEO using low-band and mid-band spectrums controlled by Mobile Network Operators (MNOs) in areas lacking terrestrial network coverage.

Let us delve a little deeper into the companies' competitive dynamics to understand which of the two is relatively better placed in the industry.

The Case for SPCX

SpaceX has transformed the launch industry through its reusable Falcon 9 rockets, significantly reducing launch costs and increasing mission frequency. The company now conducts more launches annually than any of its global competitors, giving it a commanding share of the commercial launch market. In addition, Starlink provides recurring subscription income and potentially higher long-term margins. The business also benefits from a powerful competitive advantage. SpaceX can launch its own satellites at a fraction of the cost of its competitors, allowing Starlink to expand its network faster and more efficiently. As global demand for reliable broadband connectivity increases, Starlink's prospects become solid.

The Elon Musk-led company is aiming to evolve into a vertically integrated artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure company by combining advanced AI models, large-scale computing capabilities and satellite connectivity under one umbrella. The transformation is likely to unlock a significantly larger addressable market while diversifying the company's revenue base beyond launch services and Starlink. As part of the transition, xAI's flagship chatbot, Grok, operates under the SpaceXAI brand. The integration is expected to strengthen collaboration between the company's AI software, computing infrastructure and satellite network, creating a differentiated ecosystem that few competitors can match.

The company plans to deploy AI compute satellites as early as 2028, effectively creating space-based data centers capable of delivering large-scale computing capacity. This initiative leverages SpaceX's leadership in satellite deployment while addressing the growing demand for AI computing resources. Alongside its satellite ambitions, SpaceX continues to expand its Colossus data center platform, strengthening its position in AI infrastructure. SpaceX has also signed a definitive agreement to acquire Anysphere in an all-stock deal valued at $60 billion. The buyout of a startup firm behind the rapidly growing AI coding assistant Cursor is primarily aimed at gaining a firmer footing in the enterprise AI market.

However, SpaceX is scaling several capital-intensive platforms simultaneously. The company is investing heavily in COLOSSUS, COLOSSUS II, Grok, enterprise offerings, compute services and future orbital AI compute. Management expects a multi-year investment cycle until sustained positive segment-adjusted EBITDA is realized. The strategy may create a cost advantage if compute, energy and launch assets integrate as planned. Until then, AI adds uncertainty to margins, capital needs and consolidated earnings quality.

AT&T (NYSE:T) has begun building a new 54 acre global headquarters campus in Plano, Texas for its Dallas Fort Worth workforce.

The project is planned as a highly connected workspace that uses AT&T fiber optic and 5G infrastructure across the consolidated campus.

Teams currently spread across multiple Dallas Fort Worth locations are expected to be brought together at the Plano site once construction is completed.

The new Plano headquarters project, and what it signals about how AT&T wants its people to work, sits within a wider pattern our research has been tracking for this business. We have also spotted 3 warning signs worth knowing about at AT&T.

This telecom giant is far from the only business exposed to the build out of critical communications infrastructure, and a wider peer group might be worth your time to review through 43 power grid technology and infrastructure stocks.

NYSE:T Earnings & Revenue Growth as at Nov 2026

AT&T is a large US telecom provider with a market value of about $147.8b, and this headquarters build sits alongside its core role of supplying fiber and wireless connectivity that underpins much of the data traffic running through North Texas and beyond.

4 things going right for AT&T that this headline doesn't cover.

What AT&T's Plano campus signals about the fiber and 5G Narrative

The investment story for AT&T rests on whether a large scale connectivity platform can squeeze more value from fiber and 5G while holding the cost base in check, and this campus build is one more test of that idea in physical form.

"The push toward network convergence across fiber, wireless and fixed wireless is progressing, with converged consumer households already above 40% of the internet base…"

See how the full story points towards a $27.59 fair value for AT&T.

The Plano headquarters fits the bullish view that AT&T is building a tightly integrated network plus service platform rather than a loose collection of assets. A single, highly wired campus supports the fiber led convergence story and the heavy use of digital tools that analysts already assume in their expectations for recurring service revenue and earnings quality.

Yet this development also highlights the bear arguments around capital intensity and execution risk that sit beside AT&T's high debt and thinner 10.2% profit margin, especially versus peers like Verizon and T Mobile. Consolidation into Plano only pays off if it helps retire legacy processes, supports the copper phase out and keeps wage and support costs from drifting higher in a more complex, tech heavy environment.

AT&T expects free cash flow of $21 billion or more by 2028, while General Mills guides for lower operating profit this fiscal year as it pays down debt.

SpaceX's push into wireless is the main new risk to AT&T's cash flow, and General Mills' debt sits above its own target.

General Mills (GIS:NYSE) declared another $0.61 quarterly dividend on Sept. 29. That's the same rate as before, a 7.0% yield.

AT&T (T:NYSE) isn't raising its dividend either. With its third-quarter results on Oct. 21, it said it plans to keep paying $1.11 a share a year, a 5.2% yield.

So with neither dividend growing, which is the better high-yield buy?

6 safe dividend stocks paying retirees 6%+ yields

There are over 100 stocks paying 6%+ annual dividends today.

But after an extensive investment review leveraging TIKR's proprietary data, we now believe only six of them are truly safe for retirees.

They're all yours for free as part of our new investment report, which you can access right here.

AT&T is trading copper for fiber

AT&T's dividend per share fell from $2.08 in fiscal 2020 to $1.11 in fiscal 2025, which explains the negative 5-year rate. What's left is well-covered. It used 44% of free cash flow over the twelve months to Sept. 30, 2026, and 46% on analysts' fiscal 2026 consensus. Since fiscal 2023, the dividend has cost just over $8 billion a year, under half of free cash flow every year:

AT&T (T): free cash flow vs. dividends paid, $ billions, fiscal 2016–2025 (TIKR)

That cash comes from a business that's moving from copper to fiber. Third-quarter revenue rose 5.3% from a year earlier to $32.3 billion. AT&T had a record 769,000 internet net adds in what it calls Advanced Connectivity, while Legacy revenue fell 24.5%.

On the third-quarter call, CEO John Stankey called "a fiber-fed broadband customer with a great wireless service on top of it" the industry's most durable combination. SpaceX wants to compete for the wireless half of that. AT&T stock fell 8% on Oct. 23 after Bloomberg reported that SpaceX is in talks for access to at least 80,000 US cell sites.

General Mills is paying down debt first

General Mills is also holding its dividend flat, but its reason is debt. CFO Kofi Bruce said on the Sept. 23 first-quarter call, "we remain fully committed to our dividend, and in the near term, we expect to maintain the current rate per share while we prioritize deleverage." He expects it to take "at least a couple of years" to get back to the company's 3x net debt to EBITDA target.

AT&T Lays the First Fiber at Its 54-Acre Plano Campus, Reinforcing Its Long-Term Investment in North Texas

PLANO, Texas, Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AT&T (NYSE: T) today broke ground on its new global headquarters in Plano, Texas, marking the start of construction with a distinct AT&T milestone: the installation of the campus's first fiber connection.

The new headquarters represents a strategic investment in AT&T's people, culture, and employee experience. Spanning 54 acres and 2.2 million square feet, the seven-building campus will bring AT&T's Dallas-Fort Worth teams together in an integrated, horizontal headquarters designed to foster collaboration and innovation. With workspaces and amenities shaped around employees' needs, the campus will also help AT&T attract, develop, and retain talent for the future.

Engineered as a workplace of the future, the new headquarters will demonstrate what AT&T connectivity makes possible at scale. AT&T fiber and wireless will provide the speed, capacity and low latency needed for AI, real-time collaboration, and emerging workplace technologies. An approximately 250-foot working cell tower, together with fiber and 5G throughout the campus, will provide advanced connectivity for employees and improve wireless connectivity in the surrounding community. The tower will also serve as a recognizable Plano landmark and symbol of AT&T's commitment to a more connected future.

To celebrate the first fiber connection, AT&T executives and employees were joined by Plano Mayor John Muns; Scott Armstrong, principal at Gensler; Eric Hage, president of KDC; and Andy Leatherman, vice chairman at CBRE.

John Stankey, chairman and CEO of AT&T, spoke about what the campus will mean for the company: "Our new headquarters in Plano is an investment for our current and future employees, and our North Texas community. With this new campus, we're creating the environment that makes life better, drives collaboration and serves our customers for decades to come."

John Muns, mayor of Plano, said, "Today marks an exciting milestone for AT&T and the City of Plano," said Mayor John Muns. "This new global headquarters represents a significant investment in our community and reinforces Plano's reputation as a place where businesses can grow and succeed. We're proud to see this project taking shape and the opportunities it will bring to Plano."

Scott Armstrong, principal at Gensler, said, "Great workplaces do more than support the way people work. They create connections, strengthen culture, and provide a sense of belonging. The vision for AT&T's new headquarters creates a world-class destination where innovative workplaces, exceptional amenities, and thoughtfully designed experiences come together to support people in new ways. It is a forward-looking campus that honors the strength of AT&T's legacy while creating an environment designed to inspire connection, innovation, and the possibilities of what comes next."
